::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Can you provide me an example of quantifiers with their scopes overlapping?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4919880/can-you-provide-me-an-example-of-quantifiers-with-their-scopes-overlapping), asked by [Bob Marley](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/801877/bob-marley) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2024-05-20; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> [![Rosen Discrete Math Textbook][q-1]][q-1]
>
> Screenshot comes from Rosen's Discrete Math Textbook. 
>
> Scope (as per textbook): The part of a logical expression to which a quantifier is applied is called the scope of this quantifier.
>
> The textbook gives the example of $\exists x(P(x)\land Q(x)) \lor \forall xR(x)$ and explains that scope of the first quantifer doesn't overlap with the the scope of the 2nd quantifier since the first quantifier's scope is limited to $P(x)\land Q(x)$, whereas the 2nd quantifier's scope is limited to $R(x)$. 
>
>
> Because the scope's don't overlap, textbook says that we could express it using 2 different variables x & y, as $\exists x(P(x)\land Q(x)) \lor \forall yR(y)$. However, they also mention:
>
> > The reader should be aware that in common usage, the same letter is often used to represent variables bound by different quantifiers with scopes that do not overlap.
>
> Kindly could someone provide a good example of an expression where the quantifiers' scopes do overlap? 
>
>   [q-1]: Qp51ivnZ.png
:::

Here is an example of a statement where quantifiers overlap and the symbol is repeated.

**Claim.** $-1$ is the only odd integer.

_Proof._ Suppose that $a$ is an odd integer. By definition, there exists an integer $a$ such that $a=2a+1$. By algebra, $a=-1$.

This is, of course, false. The problem is that the letter used for the existential quantifier was the same as the universal quantifier surrounding the claim.
